title: Hilda of Whitby
hookLine: a wise abbess who led a monastery of men and women and hosted a great synod

cards: In a house in the north of England, people keep arriving with questions for one woman. Ordinary people come, Bede says. So do kings and princes.
They want to know what she thinks. She isn't a bishop or a queen. She's an abbess, and the people in her care have their own name for her.

teach.h: A HOUSE OF MEN AND WOMEN.
teach.b: Her name was Hilda, and she led the monastery at Whitby. It was a community of both men and women, under one abbess. Bede writes about her with real warmth.
Her wisdom was so well known, he says, that rulers sought her counsel. She taught the people in her care to study the scriptures and to do what's right.

teach.h: NO ONE RICH, NO ONE POOR.
teach.b: She modeled the house on the earliest church in the Book of Acts, where no one was rich and no one was poor, because everything was shared.
And everyone who knew her called her mother.
Whitby is also where a great meeting happened, the synod of Whitby. The churches in the north had a problem. Some kept the customs they'd learned from the Irish monks of Iona, Columba's island.
Others kept the customs of Rome. They didn't even agree on the date of Easter, so in one royal household, Bede says, one person could still be fasting while another was already celebrating.
The king called both sides together at Hilda's house. Each side made its case. Hilda and her community held with the Irish custom.

The king listened, and chose the Roman one, saying he would side with Peter, who holds the keys of heaven. Some who had argued for the Irish way went home to Iona. Bede doesn't record a word Hilda said that day.
Her side lost, and she stayed, and went on leading her house.

how: Anglican, Catholic and Orthodox Christians remember Saint Hilda of Whitby, and schools, colleges and churches in England and beyond bear her name.

the abbess of Whitby whom everyone called mother

games.q: you're the king. at Hilda's house, one side argues for the customs of Iona, the other for the customs of Rome. you have to choose. what do you do?

let each side keep its own.
games.why: the king chose Rome, saying he would side with Peter, who holds the keys. some went home to Iona; Hilda stayed and led her house.

practice: Think of a woman whose judgment you trust: a grandmother, a teacher, a friend, someone at work.

Notice what makes her wise, how she listens, what she's lived through, how little she rushes, and shape one real question you've been carrying into a single sentence, the kind you'd only ask someone like her.
If you pray, give thanks for her; if not, just keep her face in mind.

wordCard.voice: Hilda. The abbess of Whitby kings came to for counsel, whose house hosted the great argument, and whom everyone called mother. That ends a week of Brigid, Benedict, Scholastica, Columba, Gregory and Augustine.
